extraction_text: Brahma describes the hierarchy and kingship among various categories in the universe.

Brahma lists examples of kingship: Kshatriya among humans, elephant among mounts, lion among forest animals, goat among sacrificial animals, snake among cave dwellers, bull among cattle, man among women.
Brahma enumerates tree kings: Banyan, Jambu, Peepal, Silk-cotton, Shinshupa, Sheep-horn tree, and Bamboo.
Brahma names mountain kings: Himalayas, Pariyatra, Sahya, Vindhya, Trikuta, White Mountain, Green Mountain, Varsha, and Kashthavata.

Brahma identifies celestial and divine kings: Sun among planets, Moon among constellations, Yama among ancestors, Ocean among rivers, Varuna among waters, Mitra among beings, Arka among heat, Moon among luminaries, Fire among elements, Brihaspati among Brahmins, Soma among herbs, Vishnu among the strong, Vishvakarma among forms, Shiva among beasts, Sacrifice among gifts, Sages among Vedas, North among directions, Soma among Brahmins, Kubera among Yakshas, Indra among gods, Creation among all things, Prajapati among beings.

Brahma declares the supreme kingship: The Great Self (Atman) composed of Brahman is king of all, with none higher than himself or Vishnu; Vishnu, composed of Brahman, is king of kings, known as Ishvara, Lord, and Prajapati.

attributes.relationships: Vishnu is identified as the supreme king and lord over all beings.

extraction_text: Brahma states Vishnu's dominion: He is the lord of humans, Kinnaras, Yakshas, Gandharvas, snakes, Rakshasas, gods, Danavas, and Nagas.

Brahma describes the most enchanting woman: The great goddess Parvati, with beautiful eyes, is most beloved by amorous men; among women, Uma is most auspicious; among pleasure-giving women, Apsaras are most charming.
Brahma explains the duty of kings: Kings love Dharma, Brahmins are marked by Dharma, so kings should strive to protect Brahmins.

attributes.relationship: Kings and Brahmins are linked through Dharma

extraction_text: Brahma outlines consequences for kings: If good people are distressed in a king's realm, the king fails his duty and falls after death; if protected, the king is noble, enjoys happiness in life, and attains infinite bliss after death.

Brahma describes the eternal marks of Dharma and other entities: Dharma is marked by non-violence, Adharma by violence; gods by radiance, humans by actions, space by sound, wind by touch, light by color, water by taste, earth by smell, speech by truth, mind by thought or consciousness, consciousness by discernment, the great by meditation, the unmanifest by good people, Yoga by activity, knowledge by renunciation.
Brahma concludes: Therefore, wise people praise knowledge and renounce everything; through knowledge, renouncers attain the supreme goal.

attributes.conclusion: Knowledge leads to renunciation and the supreme goal

extraction_text: He transcends opposition, darkness, death, and aging.

extraction_text: The senses and their corresponding elements are described: smell (earth/nose), taste (water/tongue), form (light/eyes), touch (wind/skin), sound (space/ears), thought (mind/intellect).
The knower of the field (soul) is without qualities and cannot be grasped by qualities; it is known only through knowledge.
The unmanifest (primordial matter) resides in the field (body), with qualities arising and ceasing, yet the knower perceives it.
The knower of the field, perceiving all movements of qualities, knows the truth and attains the supreme greatness beyond qualities.
One who knows the truth abandons qualities and entities, eliminates sin, and enters the knower of the field.

Food is the foremost of all eatables, and water is the foremost of all drinkables.
The fig tree is the foremost of all immovable things, said to be the first produced and always a sacred place of Brahma.

extraction_text: Household life is the foremost of all modes of life. The unmanifest (primordial matter) is the origin of the world and the end of everything.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Metaphysical concepts of origin and end

extraction_text: The sun setting ends the day; the sun rising ends the night. The end of happiness is pain; the end of pain is happiness.
All accumulations end in exhaustion, all ascents in a fall, all unions in separation, all life in death.
All creation ends in destruction, all beings in death. In this world, all animals and immovable things are impermanent.
Sacrifices, gifts, austerities, study, vows, and observances all end in destruction; only knowledge has no end.
Therefore, one whose soul is calm, concentrated, free from selfishness and egoism, such a person, through pure knowledge, is freed from all sins.
This concludes chapter 44 of the Ashvamedha Parva in the Mahabharata.
Brahma describes the wheel of time: with wisdom as its essence, thought as its axle, senses as its connections, five elements as its spokes, moments as its rim.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Metaphorical description of time with divine and cosmic elements

extraction_text: The wheel of time is filled with old age and sorrow, accompanied by disease and calamity, based on place and time, with toil and fatigue as its sound.
The wheel of time turns with day and night as its motion, cold and heat as its circumference, pleasure and pain as its dirt, hunger and thirst as its nails.
The wheel of time has sunlight and shadow as its tracks, moments as its tremors, filled with terrible deluded people, always revolving without consciousness.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Personification of time's motion and effects

extraction_text: The wheel of time is measured by months and fortnights, moves with time, uneven. With accumulated darkness as mire, impulsive passion as motive power.
The wheel of time has the adornments of beings as its highlights, various qualities as its circumference, noise as its hub, various sorrows as its revolution.
The wheel of time possesses action and means, extends with desire, counted by greed and craving, with ignorance as its source.
The wheel of time has fear and folly as attendants, the folly of beings as its maker, joy and delight as its sustainer, desire and anger as its controllers.
The wheel of time has greatness as its origin, various specialities as its end, ceaselessly produced and destroyed, swift as thought, tirelessly revolving.
One should know the wheel of time as unconscious, dependent on opposites, releasing and withdrawing the worlds together with the gods.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Time's power over gods and worlds

extraction_text: A person who truly knows the operation and cessation of the wheel of time does not fall into ignorance among beings.
A sage, free from all afflictions, beyond all opposites, free from all sins, attains the supreme abode.
The four stages of life (householder, student, forest-dweller, ascetic) are described, with the householder stage as the foundation.
A person born in a virtuous family undergoes purification rituals, observes vows, studies the Vedas, and returns home.
A householder loves his wife, restrains himself, maintains good conduct, controls senses, has faith, and performs the five great sacrifices.
A sage who restrains his limbs, speech, and body is considered excellent.
A person wears the sacred thread, white clothes, observes pure vows, restrains himself, gives generously, and associates with sages.
A sage controls sexual and food desires, is friendly to all, maintains excellent conduct, and carries a bamboo staff and water pot.
Six modes of conduct are described: studying, teaching, performing sacrifices for oneself and others, giving, and receiving gifts.
Three modes (performing sacrifices for others, teaching, receiving pure gifts) constitute the Brahmin's way of life.
A sage who is self-controlled, friendly, treats all beings equally with tolerance, and knows dharma should diligently perform these three duties.
A Brahmin who lives at home, strictly observes vows, maintains purity, and diligently performs all duties wins heaven.

attributes.action: Achieving heavenly reward through proper conduct

extraction_text: Brahma describes the path of a student: studying the Vedas according to rules, observing celibacy, controlling senses, serving the teacher's interests, and being pure in body and mind.
A student eats food with the teacher's permission, without complaint, eating begged offerings while standing, sitting, or walking.
A twice-born's clothing should be of linen, cotton, deerskin, or reddish-brown color, with a munja grass belt, hair tuft, daily bathing, sacred thread, Vedic study, and abandonment of desires.
A celibate student who meditates, controls sexual desire, wins heaven, attains supreme status, and is freed from the cycle of birth and death.

After various purification rituals and observing celibacy, a sage leaves the village to become a forest-dweller, wearing animal skin or bark, performing morning purification, and living permanently in the forest.
